(a) In General.—Not later than 2 years after the date of enactment of this Act, the Federal Judicial Center, using existing resources, shall develop recommended best practices for—
        (1) the seizure of information and media storing the information; and 
        (2) the securing of the information and media once seized.  
    (b) Updates.—The Federal Judicial Center shall update the recommended best practices developed under subsection (a) from time to time. 
    (c) Congressional Submissions.—The Federal Judicial Center shall provide a copy of the recommendations developed under subsection (a), and any updates made under subsection (b), to the—
        (1) Committee on the Judiciary of the Senate; and 
        (2) Committee on the Judiciary of the House of Representatives.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that developing recommended best practices and submitting them to committees is a consultative process. But the Federal Judicial Center is a federal judicial-branch agency and the only recipients are congressional Judiciary Committees, all inside the federal government. The section requires no public comment, rulemaking, outside advisory body, consultation with non-federal parties, or right to sue.

qwen_block.w: This section requires the Federal Judicial Center to submit reports to congressional committees. Congress is part of the federal government, so reporting to it is an internal government action, not participation by outside parties. There is no requirement for consultation with states, the public, or other non-federal entities.
qwen_block.s: The Federal Judicial Center shall provide a copy of the recommendations developed under subsection (a), and any updates made under subsection (b), to the— (1) Committee on the Judiciary of the Senate; and (2) Committee on the Judiciary of the House of Representatives.

opus.w: Every actor in this section is federal: the Federal Judicial Center writes the best practices and sends them to the Senate and House Judiciary Committees. Reports to Congress do not count as participation. Writing non-binding recommended best practices is not rulemaking, and the section has no comment period, hearing, outside advisory body or consultation with non-federal parties.
opus.s: The Federal Judicial Center shall provide a copy of the recommendations developed under subsection (a), and any updates made under subsection (b), to the—
opus.b: Some readers might count the Federal Judicial Center's work on "best practices" as rulemaking, or count sending them to the Judiciary Committees as participation. Neither applies. The Center is a federal judicial agency, and it is only writing non-binding recommendations, not issuing regulations. The Judiciary Committees are part of Congress, so they are inside the federal government. No state, expert, company or member of the public is consulted at any point.

qwen_chat.w: This section requires the Federal Judicial Center to develop best practices and submit them to congressional committees. Congress is part of the federal government, so reporting to it is internal government communication, not participation by outside parties. The text does not require consultation with states, tribes, the public, or other non-federal entities.
qwen_chat.s: The Federal Judicial Center shall provide a copy of the recommendations developed under subsection (a), and any updates made under subsection (b), to the— (1) Committee on the Judiciary of the Senate; and (2) Committee on the Judiciary of the House of Representatives.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the Federal Judicial Center is an independent agency and thus "outside" the executive branch, or that developing best practices involves consulting with judges or experts. However, the text does not mention any consultation with outside parties (judges, experts, public). It only mandates the creation of recommendations and their submission to Congress. Congress is inside the federal government. Therefore, there is no participation by non-federal entities.
